what_its_for: Lamotrigine is used to treat epilepsy (seizures) in adults and children. It is also used to help prevent mood episodes — such as depression, mania, or mixed episodes — in adults with bipolar disorder. It works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain.
how_to_take: Take lamotrigine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow regular tablets whole with water. If you have chewable or dissoluble tablets, you can chew them, dissolve them in water, or swallow them whole. Extended-release tablets (XR) must be swallowed whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. Always take this medicine at the same time each day. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a very low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks. This is very important to lower your risk of a serious skin rash. The dose varies widely depending on your condition, your age, other medicines you take, and how well your body responds. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine on your own — always talk to your doctor first. Stopping suddenly can cause seizures.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss several doses in a row, call your doctor before restarting, because your doctor may need to restart you at a lower dose to reduce the risk of a skin rash.
storage: Store lamotrigine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking lamotrigine, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness and may raise your risk of seizures. Be careful driving, operating machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid stopping this medicine suddenly. Tell your doctor before starting any new medicines — including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements — because many medicines can change how lamotrigine works. Oral contraceptives (birth control pills) can lower lamotrigine levels in your blood, so talk to your doctor if you start or stop birth control.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help RIGHT AWAY if you notice: a skin rash of any kind (this can be a sign of a rare but life-threatening reaction — do not wait to see if it goes away on your own); blistering, peeling, or sores inside your mouth; swollen lymph nodes; fever, flu-like symptoms, or unusual bruising or bleeding; new or worsening depression, anxiety, agitation, or thoughts of harming yourself; confusion, difficulty concentrating, or sudden mood changes; eye pain or vision changes; or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: For seizures, it may take several weeks before you notice the full benefit because your doctor increases the dose slowly. For bipolar disorder, it can take several months of gradual dose increases before you feel the full effect. Do not get discouraged — keep taking it as directed even if you feel well.
special_populations: Children: Lamotrigine can be used in children as young as 2 years old for seizures, but the dose is carefully calculated by weight. Children may need more frequent dose adjustments. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Lamotrigine may affect the unborn baby, but stopping seizure medicine can also be dangerous. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. The dose of lamotrigine often needs to be adjusted during pregnancy. Breastfeeding: Lamotrigine passes into breast milk; talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness and may need lower doses. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease.
